title: Scott Lincicome and Jeff Ferry | Full Episode 2.21.25 | Firing Line with Margaret Hoover | PBS
channel: Firing Line with Margaret Hoover | PBS
summary: PBS Firing Line debate (Feb 2025): Lincicome argues Americans pay tariffs, which hit domestic prices, downstream manufacturers and investment; Ferry argues the cost is shared, steel tariffs paid off and revenue can be rebated.

assertions.quote: tariffs are typically paid by consumers, whether that is companies or individuals in the United States.

verdicts.note: Studies of the 2018-2019 tariffs (Amiti-Redding-Weinstein, Fajgelbaum et al., Cavallo et al.) found near-complete pass-through into US import prices with little exporter price cutting.

assertions.quote: in most cases, it is actually the American consumer, companies or individuals, paying it.

verdicts.note: Pass-through studies of 2018-2019 found foreign exporters cut prices little; US importers bore nearly all of the tariff, with partial exceptions for some Chinese goods.

assertions.quote: not just the imported goods, but the domestic ones, as well.

verdicts.note: Protected domestic producers raise prices under the tariff umbrella; the USITC found domestic steel prices rose with the 2018 tariffs.

The paper's central finding is that tariffs raise the prices of goods made at home, not just the imports they tax: 36 percent of the consumer price effect comes through domestic producers' higher imported-input costs and higher markups under weaker import competition.

assertions.quote: steel-consuming industries outnumber steel industries in terms of workers by 70 to 1

verdicts.note: Flaaen and Pierce (Fed, 2019) found the 2018-2019 tariffs' input-cost and retaliation effects outweighed import protection, for a net loss of manufacturing jobs.

assertions.quote: the 25% steel tariff led to the prices paid in America by steel buyers to rise by 2.4 percent.

verdicts.note: The USITC found the Section 232 tariffs raised domestic steel output and prices modestly, but the same report found larger output losses in steel-using industries.

assertions.quote: When Trump levied tariffs in 2018 and 2019, consumer price inflation actually fell. It didn't rise.

verdicts.note: Tariffed goods rose 10-30 percent in price but were a small share of the basket, so the aggregate CPI effect was a few tenths of a point, hard to see in headline figures.

The authors' earlier work found foreign exporters did not lower prices at all in 2018-2019, so the tariffs passed 100 percent into U.S. import prices; this shows the price-raising mechanism operated but the post does not measure the effect on overall consumer inflation, and those tariffs were far smaller than the 2025 ones.

assertions.quote: not a day goes by that there's not some story about investors holding back investment because of tariff-related uncertainty.

verdicts.note: Fed research (Caldara et al. 2020) estimated 2018-2019 trade-policy uncertainty cut US investment by about 1 percent, and retaliation cut farm and manufacturing exports.

assertions.quote: when you actually apply those tariffs, imports go down. So you actually have a shrinking tax base

verdicts.note: Imports are about 3 trillion dollars against roughly 2.2 trillion of income tax revenue, and rates high enough to close the gap would cut imports sharply; PWBM and Tax Foundation reach the same conclusion.

assertions.quote: You can then use that money to give everybody who's earning less than $1 million a year a $1,200 cut in their income tax.

verdicts.note: Rebating tariff revenue returns the transfer part of the cost, but Fajgelbaum et al. found the 2018-2019 tariffs still left a net loss after revenue because of deadweight and retaliation losses.

assertions.quote: it plus the retaliation that it engendered contributed to the Great Depression. It didn't cause it.

verdicts.note: Most economic historians rate Smoot-Hawley and the retaliation it triggered as a secondary factor that deepened the Depression by collapsing trade, with monetary contraction as the main cause.
